Wildfires can also damage solar panels and equipment

Wildfires may be adversely affecting solar power generation worldwide. According to a recent study published in Nature, smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours (TWh) over five months. The researchers estimated that the reduction amounted to about 2.8% of the solar electricity generated across the two regions during that period.The report also estimated that the decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires that blocked or scattered sunlight before it could reach solar panels, though they noted significant uncertainty around the estimates.The 2023 Canadian wildfire season produced large amounts of smoke that travelled across North America and reached parts of Europe. The researchers modelled the atmospheric effects of the wildfire emissions over five months to estimate their impact on solar electricity generation.Sunlight is absorbed and scattered by particles in the atmosphere. This results in less sunlight reaching the solar panels, and installations producing less electricity even if the panels themselves are not directly affected by fire.The findings also show how the effects of wildfires can extend beyond areas immediately surrounding the fires. Solar farms, commercial installations and rooftop systems can all be affected when smoke moves through the atmosphere above them.Wildfire smoke is not the only source of air pollution that decreases the productivity of solar panel arrays. Pollution particles (particulate matter) released into the air by automobiles and coal-burning electrical generators may decrease how much sunlight enters your solar array.Dust can affect panels in different ways by settling directly on the panel surface . Dust accumulation from construction and mining activities can reduce electricity generation if panels are not cleaned.Improved solar-power forecasting can help grid operators prepare for generation changes caused by smoke. More accurate forecasts can help operators anticipate declines in solar output and arrange alternative electricity sources to maintain the balance between supply and demand.According to Cornell University, researchers studied a machine learning model for predicting solar energy production during certain extreme wildfire smoke OPS events in 2025. Researchers indicated that the model has more detail and accuracy than the New York grid operator's forecasts.Emissions from automobiles and factories are a source of atmospheric pollution. These can be reduced with improved dust management at solar farms. This will limit the effects of pollution on the farms’ ability to generate electricity.Wildfire smoke can affect solar generation without physically damaging an installation, but fires can also directly threaten solar farms. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified wildfire damage as a risk to photovoltaic systems, including potential damage to panels and components used to operate them.A solar farm owned by a French company Luxel was affected by a wildfire last month. The fire broke out in southern France in July 2026. About 100 of the 43,500 panels and some cables were damaged in the blaze, while the transformers and inverters were not harmed.Vegetation management around the site helped limit the fire's reach. Luxel said that regular clearing work, including a 50-meter perimeter around the fences, helped prevent flames from reaching most of the installation.The US Department of Energy recommends maintaining defensible space around solar installations in areas exposed to wildfire risk. Its measures include managing vegetation, paving areas around critical equipment, placing important electrical components in fire-resistant containers, maintaining access for firefighters and keeping an updated wildfire emergency-response plan.The Canadian wildfire study illustrates how fires can affect solar power production without reaching a solar energy facility, and physical damage to infrastructure is an additional risk to facilities built in wildland-urban interface areas.
Article Summary: Smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours. The decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires.

Article Title: Startup founded by three Harvard dropouts that tech investors warned of saying 'don’t back kids in chips' is pulling talent from Nvidia; engineer says ...
Article Text:
Etched co-founders Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu. (Image source: WSJ)

Investors once warned ‘Don’t back the kids in chips’

Etched is hiring from Nvidia

A chip startup once viewed by investors as too inexperienced to take on the semiconductor industry is now pulling engineers from Nvidia and other major chip companies, as it moves closer to becoming a serious player in AI hardware. Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative-trading firm Jane Street as its first customer, booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. The hiring trend has also surprised some of its new employees. Former Nvidia systems engineer Anthony Gamerman said he kept hearing about colleagues leaving Nvidia for Etched. “One leaves, and then another one, you hear a couple weeks later, and you go, ‘Whoa, I can’t believe so-and-so is heading over to Etched,’” he said.Etched was started by Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu, who are all 24 years old. The company initially struggled to attract investors because of the founders' limited experience in semiconductor hardware.Sonya Huang, a general partner at Sequoia Capital, described the concern among investors at the time. “Among tech investors, the prevailing wisdom was ‘don’t back the kids in chips,’” Huang said.She added that investors believed young founders could succeed in internet businesses but faced much bigger challenges when building semiconductor hardware.Etched has since raised nearly $2 billion, including a new $700 million funding round led by Jane Street that values the company at $21 billion.The startup has built a team with significant semiconductor experience. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia, according to Etched. The company has also hired engineers from other established semiconductor firms.Brian Loiler, who spent nearly 23 years at Nvidia, joined Etched to work on its servers and racks. He has since helped recruit about a dozen Nvidia engineers to the startup, with some turning down counteroffers. Jimmy Daley, a former Nvidia vice president of data-center systems engineering who retired in July, is also an investor in Etched.The company has developed AI processors designed specifically for this workload. Its first customer is Jane Street, a quantitative trading firm that uses powerful computing systems to run trading models quickly. Etched says it has already started shipping its chips and took just 44 days to get its test chips running inference workloads after receiving them from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.“We may be the only AI chip that was built by a startup that was successful on the first try,” Etched co-founder and president Robert Wachen said.
Article Summary: Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative- trading firm Jane Street as its first customer. The company has booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia.

Article Title: One of world’s most popular festivals has a ‘privacy warning’ for smart AI glasses wearers
Article Text:
Clarifying the rules on consent and wearable tech

The growing controversy over discreet cameras

Amid the concerns over breach of privacy by smart spectacles such as Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, Burning Man 2026 has officially permitted them but the event organisers are delivering a warning directive to attendees: respect personal boundaries and obtain explicit consent before recording anyone. Citing the official Burning Man 2026 Survival Guide, Business Insider reports that attendees must ask for and receive permission from every person captured within their recording frame, including individuals in the background as well as direct subjects, before operating cellphones, digital cameras, or smart eyewear. The mandate covers both private moments and artistic installations across the desert gathering.A spokesperson for the Burning Man Project explained to the publication that while the festival’s baseline privacy and consent standards are longstanding, the 2026 documentation was updated to explicitly name smart eyewear due to rapid advancements in wearable tech. The spokesperson emphasised that the organisation prioritises attendee privacy and insists that all media recording practices respect personal boundaries and the collective experience across Black Rock City.The policy shift highlights how smart frames are moving into the cultural mainstream while sparking discussions around individual privacy.Hardware like Meta’s Ray-Ban and Oakley AI glasses resemble everyday frames while concealing built-in microphones, speakers, artificial intelligence assistants and high-definition cameras. While fans praise the ability to capture first-person video hands-free without reaching for a smartphone, the hidden cameras have sparked major privacy backlash.The devices feature a white LED indicator that illuminates during recording, but bystanders frequently overlook it. Some users have deliberately placed stickers over the light or altered the hardware to disable it, leading Meta to issue a mandatory software patch to prevent tampering.Meta committed to scrubbing harassing footage recorded covertly on its hardware, though reports have uncovered numerous violating videos that stayed active online for weeks after the enforcement was announced. Meta stated it has removed thousands of improper posts and took down additional videos once alerted.Burning Man 2026 takes place from August 31 through September 7 in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert.
Article Summary: Burning Man 2026 has officially permitted smart eyewear. But the event organisers are delivering a warning directive to attendees: respect personal boundaries and obtain explicit consent before recording anyone. The mandate covers both private moments and artistic installations across the desert gathering.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Andrew Carnegie: No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it
Article Text:
Andrew Carnegie

What Andrew Carnegie's quote implies

Why the quote still matters

Andrew Carnegie's life and self-motivation

Legendary industrialist Andrew Carnegie is remembered for his thoughts on leadership, teamwork and success. One of his widely cited quotes focuses on an important lesson for anyone trying to lead: “No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it. ” The quote highlights the importance of trusting others, sharing responsibility and giving credit to a team. Its message remains relevant in workplaces and organisations, where effective leadership often depends on collaboration rather than individual achievement.Andrew Carnegie’s quote suggests that leadership is not about doing every task alone or taking credit for every success. A person may have strong skills, but leading others also requires the ability to trust a team and allow people to contribute.The quote also points to the importance of recognising the efforts of others. A leader who takes all the credit can weaken teamwork, while one who acknowledges contributions can build trust and encourage people to perform better.The quote has a simple lesson for leaders: You don’t have to do it all yourself to be successful. Today, leaders in the workplace often have to delegate, trust their teams and give credit for individual contributions.Sharing responsibility allows employees to use their strengths to help the organization achieve a shared purpose.Carnegie’s words therefore continue to be relevant for managers, business leaders and anyone working as part of a team.Andrew Carnegie was a Scottish-American industrialist who made his career in the steel industry in the late 19th century. Carnegie was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835, and immigrated with his family to the United States in 1848, working as a boy in a factory before moving through jobs in telegraphy and railroads. He later founded the Carnegie Steel Company, which was sold in 1901 to become part of US Steel.Often, his rise from factory worker to one of the world’s largest steel operations is mentioned alongside his thoughts on ambition, persistence, and self-driven effort. In the latter part of his life, Carnegie devoted much of his wealth to philanthropy, funding libraries, educational institutions and research organisations throughout the United States and other countries.His perspective is often referenced in discussions about workplace performance, education, and goal-setting, where consistent action and personal discipline are seen as important drivers of long-term progress and effective skill application.
Article Summary: Andrew Carnegie’s quote suggests that leadership is not about doing every task alone or taking credit for every success. The quote highlights the importance of trusting others, sharing responsibility and giving credit to a team. Its message remains relevant in workplaces and organisations where effective leadership often depends on collaboration rather than individual achievement.

Article Title: Meta sued by former manager claiming was fired for refusing to sign immigration letter for a Chinese engineer; here's all lawsuit blames the company for
Article Text:
The dispute began in 2024 when Meta and outside immigration lawyers were preparing an I-140 petition for an employee in Tillinghast’s product design organisation

Why former Meta manager is suing the company

Former manager claims Meta retaliated against him

Lawsuit accuses Meta of unequal immigration support

Meta Platforms is reportedly facing a lawsuit from a former product design manager who claims he was fired after refusing to sign an immigration support letter for a Chinese engineer. James Tillinghast filed the lawsuit on August 17 in a US District Court in New Jersey. He alleges that the letter overstated the employee’s work and that he raised concerns about how Meta provided immigration assistance to some workers. The lawsuit claims the company retaliated against him after he refused to support statements he believed were inaccurate. It accuses Meta of providing immigration support more often to some Chinese national employees than to similarly placed workers from other countries.According to the lawsuit, the dispute began in 2024 when Meta and outside immigration lawyers were preparing an I-140 petition for an employee in Tillinghast’s product design organisation. The petition sought an EB-2 National Interest Waiver, which can allow certain foreign workers to seek permanent residency in the US without a specific job offer and the usual labour certification requirement.A proposed managerial reference letter allegedly credited the employee with generating about $638 million in additional advertising revenue.It also described the worker as developing artificial intelligence tools and taking on wider leadership responsibilities. James Tillinghast claims that parts of the letter did not accurately describe the employee’s actual responsibilities.Tillinghast says engineering teams carried out much of the technical work that was attributed to the employee. He claims he discussed his concerns with Meta’s immigration legal team and worked with the employee to revise the letter.However, according to the complaint, Tillinghast eventually refused to sign statements that he believed he could not personally support.The lawsuit alleges that after he raised his concerns, his manager, Bolan Wang, provided or signed a replacement letter for the immigration petition.Tillinghast claims Meta then revoked his access to internal systems around August 29, 2024. His employment was formally ended on September 30.James Tillinghast alleges that Meta did not identify a performance improvement plan, written warning or documented performance issue when his employment ended. He claims the company later blamed his dismissal on poor performance, but argues that this explanation was a pretext for retaliation over his objections.The lawsuit names both Meta Platforms and Wang as defendants.The former manager also makes a separate allegation about Meta’s immigration assistance. According to the complaint, Meta provided company-coordinated immigration support more frequently to certain Chinese national employees than to similarly situated employees from other countries.The alleged assistance included access to immigration lawyers, help preparing and reviewing petition documents and support in obtaining managerial reference letters.Tillinghast claims Meta did not apply neutral and consistent criteria when providing these benefits.The lawsuit argues that immigration support was an employment-related benefit and that his objections to what he believed was unequal treatment were protected under New Jersey law.
Article Summary: James Tillinghast filed the lawsuit on August 17 in a US District Court in New Jersey. He alleges that the letter overstated the employee’s work and that he raised concerns about how Meta provided immigration assistance to some workers. The lawsuit claims the company retaliated against him after he refused to support statements he believed were inaccurate.

Article Title: Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro takes a hard line against data centers; says: I have heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania that ...
Article Text:
Pennsylvania data center projects face new restrictions (Representative image)

“heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania”

“I’ve heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania as I’ve traveled our commonwealth, and I’m here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers,”

“We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers working for these big tech companies. That will not happen in the commonwealth. We have a long history in Pennsylvania of industry running roughshod over our communities to make a buck — that stops with me.”

Pennsylvania data center projects face new restrictions

Josh Shapiro changes position on data center development

“Part of the challenge here is how quickly the industry has moved,”

“And so the opposition, I think, has moved just as quickly,”

“Now it’s coming upon us and certainly others to bring the facts and the data to bear but also be out there and demonstrate how this industry invests in the communities for the long term.”

Data center proposals draw criticism from Pennsylvania governor

“I’m a hell no on that project,”

“I’m a hell no on many other projects.”

“speculators”

“They’re threatening to fundamentally change the character of our communities,

Pennsylvania data center rules put local officials in charge

“Again, there are only about five projects that have even received permits to go forward,”

“The problem is there’s 100 projects or so that are wreaking havoc on our communities that are never going to be built.

What we’re doing today is taking concrete action to listen to the voices of the people, to put local leaders back in charge of their communities and to make very, very clear what the rules of the road are to be able to do business here in Pennsylvania.”

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has ordered new restrictions on data center projects in the state. Under the new order, companies will be required to obtain local approval for such projects, while data center developments will also be removed from Pennsylvania’s fast-track permitting program. Announcing the executive order this week, Shapiro said he hadand would not allow developers or technology companies to push projects through communities without local consent.Shapiro said.Under the executive order, data center projects must first receive approval from local officials. Developers will also have to sign a legally binding order committing to requirements Shapiro outlined in February, including paying for their own power, hiring locally, maintaining transparency with local governments and meeting water-conservation standards.Shapiro also said data center projects would no longer qualify for Pennsylvania’s fast-track permitting program. The order further bars nondisclosure agreements for data center projects in the state, increasing the amount of information that developers will have to make available during the approval process.The governor said the changes were prompted by what he described as an increase in speculative proposals. After the state announced two major Amazon-backed data center projects last year, Shapiro said Pennsylvania had received a large number of additional proposals, including projects he said were unlikely to be built.Shapiro's latest position represents a change from his earlier approach to data center development. Earlier this year, while introducing guidelines for the industry, he argued that Pennsylvania should play a role in the competition for artificial intelligence development and said data centers were an important part of the AI economy.He also stressed at the time that the state needed to be selective about which projects it pursued. Since then, opposition to data center developments has grown in Pennsylvania, with residents and local officials raising concerns about electricity costs, water use, environmental effects and changes to the character of communities.Josh Shapiro said conversations with residents had influenced his position.Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, said in a recent interview.he added.During his remarks, Shapiro specifically criticised data center proposals that he said had faced opposition from residents and local officials. He pointed to a project in Montgomery County, where he lives, and accused a developer of attempting to push the proposal forward despite local resistance.he said, adding,Shapiro also said Pennsylvania’s divided Legislature had not moved forward with new data center regulations, leaving him to use executive authority to establish requirements for future projects.He described some developers asand accused them of putting pressure on township officials and residents.” he said, adding that the lack of legislative progress on passing new regulations for data center development — Pennsylvania’s Legislature is under split control — left him no choice but to move on the executive order.Following his announcement, Shapiro was asked whether he regretted Pennsylvania’s earlier approach to data center development. He said only a small number of projects had received permits, while many more proposals had generated opposition despite having little prospect of being constructed.he said.The new requirements mean future data center developers in Pennsylvania will have to secure local approval, meet the governor’s conditions on power, employment and water use, and operate outside the state’s fast-track permitting process. The changes come as Shapiro faces re-election this fall and as data center development becomes a growing issue in state and local elections across the US.
Article Summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has ordered new restrictions on data center projects in the state. Under the new order, companies will be required to obtain local approval for such projects. Data center developments will also be removed from Pennsylvania’s fast-track permitting program.

Article Title: GitHub CTO apologises to developers after one of the biggest outages; admits: Since April, monthly commits have doubled, this shows pressure on our systems, but it is no excuse for outages
Article Text:
What caused the GitHub outage : an autoscaling policy watching the wrong thing

Why GitHub’s own growth has become its biggest reliability problem

GitHub has apologised for the outage that took its platform down for 7 hours and 47 minutes on August 17, and the explanation is unusually blunt. Nobody pushed bad code. Nobody fumbled a configuration change. The platform simply ran out of room.In a blog post published on August 20, Vlad Fedorov wrote that traffic hit a new peak and a critical infrastructure component in GitHub’s Central US data centre failed to scale with it. Authentication buckled first, and the pressure spread outward through github.com, Actions, APIs, pull requests, issues and Copilot. “If you were trying to ship software that day, we let you down,” the post reads.The root cause analysis points at an Istio sidecar reaching its concurrency limit while the autoscaling policy monitored the host service instead. Load balancers in Central US saturated. A latent retry bug in Visual Studio Code then amplified traffic to a single internal endpoint by roughly 10 times, which is what kept the Copilot Token Service down long after everything else came back. Engineers cut gateway retries and began rejecting inbound Copilot token requests with HTTP 403 responses.Scraping attacks on codeload endpoints made recovery messier still.At the worst of it, GitHub’s status page reported error rates near 20 percent for web and API traffic, and around 50 percent for archive and raw repository downloads. Most services recovered by 1636 UTC, Actions by 1803 UTC, and the Copilot Token Service only at 2102 UTC.Fedorov’s numbers explain the strain better than any apology. Monthly commits have climbed from 1.4 billion in April to 2.9 billion now. GitHub has added more than 3 million CPU cores and 120 petabytes of high-speed storage, and installed as much hardware as available power allowed in existing data centres. Azure now carries about 58 percent of platform load, up from 12 percent in May, and handles half of all Git operations.What comes next is a fix list: consistent retry limits, retry budgets and variable timeouts across service-to-service calls, a review of lower-priority CPU and memory alerts, and a new architecture that scales read capacity linearly with the number of readers, rolling out first to the largest monorepos.The timing is awkward. This was GitHub’s second incident in August, after an Actions failure on August 6. Cursor announced an early beta of its Origin Code Hosting product while GitHub was still dark. CloudBees CEO Moritz Plassnig wrote on LinkedIn that GitHub will not be the default choice going forward, and that the ecosystem is heading somewhere more bifurcated.
Article Summary: GitHub has apologised for the outage that took its platform down for 7 hours and 47 minutes on August 17. The root cause analysis points at an Istio sidecar reaching its concurrency limit while the autoscaling policy monitored the host service instead. GitHub has added more than 3 million CPU cores and 120 petabytes of high-speed storage.

Article Title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's Office decides to skip in-person appearance at City Council meeting for which council members complied 'pages and pages' of questions about rollout of 'second house tax' in the
Article Text:
Zohran Mamdani

Why Zohran Mamdani 's Office stayed away

Council members demand answers

Defending the release of property data

How the controversy started

Residents report confusion and privacy concerns

A pending lawsuit

The city's response and next steps

New York City Mayor administration opted not to attend Tuesday’s (August 25) City Council hearing on the rollout of the pied‑à‑terre tax, submitting a written memo instead, according to a report by Business Insider. Finance Commissioner Richard Lee said ongoing litigation prevented him from appearing in person, though he pledged to testify after the lawsuit is resolved. The levy, passed in May, imposes a progressive surcharge on non‑primary residences valued at least $5 million, and condos or co‑ops worth $1 million or more. In late July, the Department of Finance (DOF) sent letters to 17,000 addresses and published valuations for nearly 960,000 properties, sparking confusion and privacy concerns. Some residents reported receiving letters for their primary homes, while others criticized the release of property records.As reported by Business Insider, in the memo Department of Finance Commissioner Richard Lee detailed that the pending and active litigation prevented him from appearing at the hearing directly. He further added that he would have welcomed the chance to filed council members’ questions in person.Lee also noted that the Administration had asked the Council to postpone the hearing until the litigation was resolved, a request the Council declined. He said he would be prepared and willing to testify in person after August 31.Council Member Gale Brewer said her office has been “bombarded” with constituent complaints and compiled “pages and pages” of questions for the Mayor’s Office. The Council had requested an in‑person briefing, but the administration declined, citing the pending lawsuit.A central point of contention has been the DOF's release of home values and addresses ahead of the levy. In his written testimony, Lee maintained that this practice is standard, stating that the City's assessment roll is "highly accessible to the public, and it has been for many years," and pushing back directly on any suggestion otherwise. He pointed out that this property data has long been available as a searchable database on both the DOF website and NYC Open Data, with online archives dating back to fiscal year 2009, and that assessment rolls have been required to be published annually in New York for well over a century.The uproar began in late July, after the NYC Department of Finance sent letters to roughly 17,000 addresses identified as potential pied-à-terre properties based on property values and internal records. The DOF also published a broader list of more than 900,000 properties and their valuations across the city. Lee clarified in his testimony that this supplemental roll does not itself determine which properties are actually subject to the surcharge; rather, it exists to identify relevant properties and give owners a basis to challenge their valuations. Homeowners have until September 18, an extended deadline, to demonstrate that their property doesn't qualify for the tax before it could begin appearing on bills starting in 2027.Some New York residents said on social media that they mistakenly received letters intended for non-primary residences despite the property in question being their primary home, while others said they felt their privacy had been compromised by the DOF's broader records release. Council Member Gail Brewer, who represents Manhattan's Upper West Side, told Business Insider that her office has been inundated with concerned constituents in recent weeks, and that she and fellow council members had compiled extensive lists of questions about the rollout that they hoped the Mayor's Office would address.Separately, a lawsuit filed by three residents based in Manhattan and Staten Island is pending, with a court date scheduled for August 31. According to court documents, the plaintiffs are seeking emergency relief, arguing that the DOF's records release caused widespread confusion and invited unwanted scrutiny of homeowners' personal information. Their attorney, Randy Mastro, said hundreds of thousands of New York City homeowners had been drawn into a process they should never have been part of in the first place.The city has hired two dozen staffers specifically to field resident questions about the tax and assist with appeals. The policy itself, passed in May, imposes a progressive levy on non-primary homes valued by the DOF at $5 million or more, and on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. Deputy Press Secretary Matt Rauschenbach previously told Business Insider that the Law Department is prepared to vigorously defend the city against the lawsuit, and said the roughly $500 million a year the levy is expected to raise would help fund cleaner parks, safer streets, and other public investments across the city.In his written testimony, Lee also detailed the broader implementation process, noting that the surcharge was authorized under state legislation passed as part of New York's 2026/2027 budget on May 28, 2026, with rules formally adopted by DOF on July 14 following a public comment period that included a hearing held July 9. He emphasized that the initial determination letters sent to around 17,000 property owners represent only a small subset of the roughly 960,000 properties listed on the supplemental roll, and stressed that receiving a letter does not constitute a tax bill, only a preliminary determination that owners can challenge by submitting proof of primary residency or by contesting their property's valuation directly with the Tax Commission.Lee said DOF plans to continue outreach through senior centers, community meetings, its dedicated website, 311, and direct coordination with co-op and condo boards, property managers, and elected officials, describing these efforts as part of a broader commitment to ensuring homeowners have clear information and a fair opportunity to challenge determinations they believe are incorrect.
Article Summary: New York City Mayor administration opted not to attend Tuesday's City Council hearing on the rollout of the pied‑à‑terre tax. Finance Commissioner Richard Lee said ongoing litigation prevented him from appearing in person, though he pledged to testify after the lawsuit is resolved. The levy, passed in May, imposes a progressive surcharge on non‑primary residences valued at least $5 million, and condos or co‑ops worth $1 million or more.

Article Title: Most companies across America laying off employees seemingly have a new slogan: Not being replaced by ...
Article Text:
Messaging around AI-led job cuts is changing in America

From bragging AI-led job cuts to backtracking on messaging

Public anxiety growing around employment

The new ‘job cuts’ messaging: ‘Reshaping, not replacing’

CEOs across corporate America have previously highlighted the rapid advance of artificial intelligence (AI) by noting how many human workers the technology could replace. Today, amid growing public concern and rising economic nervousness, company leaders are adopting far more cautious language, avoiding direct links between workforce reductions and automation. According to a report by Axios, communications teams are caught between conflicting priorities: shareholders demand measurable evidence that heavy AI spending is boosting margins, while employees push back against being discarded in favour of automated software.The corporate narrative around generative automation has shifted dramatically over the past two years. In 2024, Klarna announced that its AI assistant took over the workload of 700 full-time support workers, with CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski boasting about doing “much more with less.”Similarly, last year, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff stated that AI helped trim customer support roles from 9,000 to roughly 5,000 because fewer people were required. Moreover, in May, Coinbase laid off about 700 staff members as CEO Brian Armstrong outlined plans to rebuild operations around smaller, “AI-native” teams.Following AI-led job cuts, executive rhetoric has become a reputational risk as worker anxiety continues to climb.Citing a CBS News/YouGov survey of 2,287 adults conducted between August 12–14 revealed that 61% of Americans expect AI to decrease overall economic opportunities, compared to only 21% who anticipate growth.Meanwhile, a Pew Research study found that 73% of Americans under the age of 30 believe AI will eliminate jobs over the next twenty years. Further reporting by consultancy Challenger, Gray & Christmas, suggests that AI remained the single most cited factor behind American job cuts in July for the fifth consecutive month, accounting for roughly 113,000 announced cuts, which is nearly 24% of all nationwide layoffs this year.Rather than framing layoffs around headcount displacement, corporate leaders now use careful phrasing to argue that automation is merely changing how work gets done. For example, Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman explicitly described 4,800 recent role eliminations as “not being replaced by AI,” while noting that the tools are redefining daily tasks.Similarly, Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal clarified that cutting 220 jobs was not driven by AI and Patreon CEO Jack Conte maintained that a 20% workforce reduction was not rooted in replacing human staff, despite AI fundamentally changing platform workflows.
Article Summary: CEOs across corporate America have previously highlighted how many human workers the technology could replace. Today, amid growing public concern and rising economic nervousness, company leaders are adopting far more cautious language. Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman explicitly described 4,800 recent role eliminations as “not being replaced by AI,” while noting that the tools are redefining daily tasks.

Article Title: SIM Card rules changing: What you can do and cannot do after August 24
Article Text:
New SIM card rules come into effect from August 24

How the new SIM verification system will work

What happens if you try to get an extra SIM

SIM card limit in India

Most parts of India: 9 mobile connections

Jammu and Kashmir: 6 mobile connections

Assam: 6 mobile connections

North-East: 6 mobile connections

SIM card rules are set to change from August 24, with telecom companies being asked to stop people from getting mobile connections beyond the permitted limit. In a circular, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has directed telecom operators to identify customers who already have the maximum number of SIM cards allowed in their name. Such customers will be informed that they cannot get another mobile connection. The new system will initially work on a post-facto basis, but operators have been told to move to real-time checks by November 30.Under the existing DoT rules, an individual can have a maximum of nine mobile connections in their name across telecom operators and licensed service areas in India. However, the limit is lower in some regions. Customers in Jammu and Kashmir, Assam and the North-East can have up to six mobile connections.From August 24, telecom companies will have to take steps to identify customers trying to get another SIM after reaching this limit. The DoT has directed operators to tell such customers that they have already reached the maximum number of mobile connections allowed and that a new connection cannot be issued.The new system will use subscriber photographs to help telecom companies identify people who have already reached the permitted SIM limit.The DoT will make representative images of subscribers who have reached the maximum limit available on the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) from August 23.Telecom operators will have to download these images every day and use them to identify customers attempting to obtain additional mobile connections.The DoT said, “From 24.8.2026 onward, TSPs shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to identify each subscriber who seeks to obtain mobile connections beyond the prescribed limit…”Initially, the system will work on a post-facto basis. This means telecom operators can carry out the verification after a new connection has been enrolled. If a connection is activated beyond the permitted limit during a day, it will have to be immediately suspended until the issue is resolved.The government has also asked telecom companies to move towards a real-time system so that excess connections can be identified and stopped during the enrolment and activation process.Here is the maximum number of mobile connections an individual can hold:Customers also have to declare the mobile connections already held in their name across different telecom operators and licensed service areas in the Customer Application Form (CAF).
Article Summary: New SIM card rules come into effect from August 24. Telecom companies will have to identify customers trying to get another SIM. They will be told that they have already reached the maximum number of connections allowed. The new system will initially work on a post-facto basis, but operators have been told to move to real-time checks.

Article Title: Sam Altman thinks that four years is too much to be in college; says that while it shouldn't be as long as it is, but is still great to ...
Article Text:
Career advice for young entrepreneurs

Balancing multiple projects

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman feels that the traditional four-year college track may no longer be necessary. According to a report by Business Insider, speaking at Internapalooza, Altman said two years at Stanford was “the exact right amount of time” for him before dropping out in 2005 to cofound Loopt, a location‑sharing app that became part of Y Combinator’s first batch. “I think I learned a lot, and it would have been like vastly diminishing returns,” he explained, adding that two more years “would have not been that great.”Altman suggested that the way the world has evolved makes four years of college excessive for some. “College just shouldn’t be as long as it is, but it was still great to meet people and kind of like live on your own and get to work on projects,” he said. He noted that many people today succeed without attending college at all, echoing views shared by his mentor Peter Thiel, who funds fellowships encouraging young people to skip or pause their studies.Altman also offered guidance to interns and aspiring founders. He cautioned against spending too much energy trying to be taken seriously. “You can sort of get a long way in life and career just by doing stuff,” he said, pointing out that AI tools now make it possible to build startups with minimal resources. For enterprise sales, however, he admitted hiring experienced professionals was sometimes necessary.Asked about the period when he was juggling OpenAI alongside other responsibilities, Altman pushed back on the common advice to focus on a single project from the start. He said it's reasonable to work on multiple things for a while, since it's often genuinely unclear early on what will succeed, what will hold someone's interest, or what will turn out to be the right fit. The real mistake, he said, comes later: once someone identifies the project they have the highest conviction in, that's the point at which they need to do the harder work of cutting loose from everything else and committing fully to it.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says four years of college may no longer be necessary. Altman dropped out of Stanford in 2005 to cofound Loopt, a location-sharing app. He said it's reasonable to work on multiple projects for a while.

Article Title: Y Combinator CEO has a message for all the founders and CEOs worried about burning too many AI tokens
Article Text:
Garry Tan backs heavy AI token spending

​

AI tokenmaxxing divides Silicon Valley

​

AI agents become part of founder workflows

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has a message for founders and CEOs concerned about the cost of using large numbers of AI tokens: “Burn, baby, burn.” Speaking on an episode of the A16z podcast this week, Tan argued that founders should spend heavily on AI agents, even when doing so can result in high annual costs.Tan said founders should give themselves permission to use large token budgets when working with AI agents, arguing that doing so can provide access to a level of AI capability that he believes will otherwise become available only in the future.“You have to tune it all the way up. You're just, like, let me load a million tokens or 800,000 tokens in,” he said about using AI agents. “When you do that, I think that you basically get to live in 2028.”Tan acknowledged that using AI agents at full capacity can be expensive. He estimated that the cost could reach tens of thousands of dollars per year, but said the spending can make sense for founders and CEOs experimenting with AI-driven workflows.“It costs, I don't know, 50 or $100,000 a year to use the agents at full strength,” he said. “It just costs like a crazy amount. But for a CEO or for a founder, it actually makes a lot of sense to do that.”His approach is to use AI agents for tasks first, then turn successful workflows into repeatable processes. Tan said founders can document the steps an agent follows and use those instructions to automate the same work in the future.“A markdown file is an employee,” he said, referring to a written set of instructions that tells an AI agent how to perform a particular job. “It's an employee that will do the job perfectly every single time, and it'll do it as many times as you want.”Tan's approach contrasts with criticism of “tokenmaxxing,” a term used for deliberately allowing AI systems or agents to consume large numbers of tokens instead of prioritising lower usage and costs.Uber's tech chief Praveen Neppalli Naga recently argued that companies may be moving away from this approach as they focus more closely on the efficiency of AI spending.“The next phase, whatever we call it, will not be characterised by who spends the most tokens, but about how people use them as efficiently as possible,” he said in a post on X.Cognition CEO Scott Wu also questioned the way some companies have approached tokenmaxxing. Speaking on a podcast in June, Wu said companies could lose sight of the relationship between token consumption and actual work produced.“It is directionally correct, but I think there are definitely some places where people have gotten carried away,” Wu said. “People are like, 'We rank our engineers by how many tokens they're spending.' Well, let's try and rank people by how much output they're actually producing.”Tan's argument focuses on using higher AI token limits as an investment in experimentation rather than treating token consumption only as a cost to minimise. He recommends first allowing agents to use the resources needed to complete a task, then converting successful processes into reusable instructions.The approach reflects a broader discussion among technology companies about how much they should spend on AI inference as increasingly capable models and agents are used for software development, research and other business tasks.
Article Summary: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan says founders should spend heavily on AI agents. He argues that doing so can provide access to a level of AI capability only available in the future. Tan's approach contrasts with criticism of “tokenmaxxing,” a term used for deliberately allowing AI systems to consume large numbers of tokens.

Article Title: Apple layoffs hit employees across teams; company confirms job cuts, says: While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also...
Article Text:
Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro

Apple Vision Pro layoffs: gaming team shut down, immersive video crew cut back

Siri job cuts explained: new AI architecture needs a different kind of engineer

Apple smart glasses take priority as Vision Pro waits for 2028

Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report by Mark Gurman. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from the Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and the software groups around it. Also caught in the round is Intelligent Systems Experience, a team inside Apple's software engineering arm that builds AI features sitting across iPhone, iPad and Mac.Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The company said it is realigning teams "to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users," and that new roles are being created even as existing ones disappear. Staff who lost jobs can apply elsewhere inside Apple. What makes this round worth reading closely is that one headcount figure is hiding two completely different stories. One team is being rebuilt. The other is being told to wait.The headset took the harder blow. Apple has largely closed the group working on Vision Pro gaming and shrunk the team producing immersive video, the 3D content Apple has used as the device's showpiece since launch. That content is expensive in a way the sales figures could not support.A single episode can run into several million dollars, shot by multiple crews of Apple staff and contractors, for an audience that stayed small. AppleInsider reported the first wave a day before Bloomberg, putting at least 60 layoffs across Apple's VR teams. Films like Submerged will still get made, just fewer of them, with outside studios expected to pick up the slack. Gaming never arrived at all. The most capable VR workaround on the platform, iVRY, still needs a Windows PC plugged in to work.Siri's situation is the opposite of a wind-down. The assistant is being rebuilt on a new technical architecture for its AI version, and that stack asks for skills the old one did not. So some roles end, resources move, and new positions open around the rebuilt assistant. Apple showed the revamped Siri at WWDC this year and a public beta is due before 2026 closes. Nobody cuts a team weeks before shipping unless the team they need looks different from the one they have.Vision Pro arrived in February 2024 at $3,499 and now sells for $3,699, close to Rs 3.2 lakh, after component costs forced a rise. Heavy, costly, thin on reasons to wear it daily. Apple insists visionOS is not going anywhere, and visionOS 27 shipped in June to prove it. A new headset is still penciled in for as late as end-2028. Meanwhile Bloomberg reports work with Samsung Display on an entry-level XR display was suspended, and Apple is aiming to announce smart glasses at WWDC 2027 and ship them that year. Those glasses will not run immersive video or heavy games.Incoming CEO John Ternus now owns the decision. Apple has not given up on a screen you wear on your face. It has given up on this one being the version people buy.
Article Summary: Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report. Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and software groups around it.

Article Title: How an accidental discovery by underconstruction Telescope in Chile captured one of Astronomy’s missing links
Article Text:
The Helix nebula, imaged here, lies 650 light-years away in the constellation Aquarius. (Image credit: Nasa)

Successful test run in the Atacama

How the Telescope uncovered the faint bow shocks

Low-cost engineering behind MOTHRA

An unfinished, custom-built observatory in Chile has unexpectedly solved one of puzzles astrophysics struggled with by directly capturing dense clouds of gas expelled by a dying star blending back into the Milky Way galaxy. As detailed in a study published in the journal Nature, the breakthrough demonstrates the exact physical mechanism through which foundational elements like carbon and oxygen, which are created deep within stellar cores, are recycled to serve as the building blocks for future stellar nurseries, planetary bodies and living organisms.The milestone occurred by chance during calibration tests in November 2025. Scientists were in the middle of assembling a composite optical instrument designed to link hundreds of commercial, off-the-shelf telephoto camera lenses into a unified composite array.With less than 200 of its targeted 1,140 lenses mounted, researchers aligned the array toward the Helix Nebula, which is an expansive, radiant ring of gas located approximately 650 light-years away from Earth. The nebula represents the remnants of a Sun-like star that cast off its external shell in its death throes.While researchers have long theorised that expelled stellar envelopes enrich the surrounding interstellar medium to seed future celestial bodies, documenting this dispersal in real time had eluded previous observational attempts.Despite running at a fraction of its final hardware capacity, the observatory detected 22 dimly illuminated arcs extending into the outer halo well beyond the Helix Nebula's primary bright ring. Researchers interpret glowing arcs as bow shocks, which resemble the wake pushed in front of a moving vessel. These are formed as dense pockets of ejected matter crash through the surrounding interstellar medium.Bow shocks situated further from the core appear distinctly smaller, softer and more fragmented, illustrating how the traveling clouds break down and dissolve into surrounding space over an estimated span of roughly 10,000 years.Commenting on the images, University of British Columbia astronomer Sun Kwok, who was not part of the research team, highlighted that the findings deliver critical new insights into how stellar mass loss interacts with interstellar space.The breakthrough imagery was recorded by the Modular Optical Telephoto Hyperspectral Robotic Array (MOTHRA), situated at Chile’s El Sauce Observatory. Constructed for a few tens of millions of dollars with financial backing from XTX Markets founder and CEO Alex Gerko, MOTHRA is scheduled for full operational completion by the end of this year.Modeled after its predecessor, the Dragonfly array in New Mexico, MOTHRA’s primary objective is tracing the faint filaments of the cosmic web that connect distant galaxies, where vast reserves of matter produce extremely faint light signals.
Article Summary: Unfinished, custom-built observatory in Chile captured dense clouds of gas expelled by a dying star blending back into the Milky Way galaxy. The breakthrough demonstrates the exact physical mechanism through which foundational elements like carbon and oxygen are recycled. The milestone occurred by chance during calibration tests in November 2025.

Article Title: Intel study reveals surge in enterprise robotics adoption but 3 gaps threaten deployment
Article Text:
Intel highlights disconnect between fleet ambition and planning

Enterprise robotics adoption is expanding, yet critical deficits across operational strategy, talent, safety frameworks and edge infrastructure risk limiting organisations from scaling successfully, according to new research commissioned by Intel. The study, titled The Robotics Readiness Gap, surveyed 800 executive decision-makers, IT managers, robotics engineers, and public sector officials across the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, China and South Korea, representing enterprises generating over $500 million in annual revenue.The findings confirm that autonomous systems are no longer treated as experimental trials, with organisations already recording tangible gains across operational speed, quality control, and workplace output.The report identifies a divide between enterprise deployment targets and organisational preparedness.The report says that 60% of senior executives anticipate running active fleets of robots within the next five years, with many projecting that full integration could double total operational productivity. While 74% of respondents believe workforce planning and robotics roadmaps will be fully unified by 2030, and 67% express confidence in supervising integrated human-robot teams by that date, only 40% currently maintain a documented, formal human-robot workforce framework.John Healy, vice president and general manager of Intel’s Industrial and Robotics Division, noted that the upcoming phase of robotics deployment will not hinge on basic technical capability, but on whether enterprises are prepared to scale. He noted that businesses embedding robotics and Physical AI directly into their primary workflows – not as add-ons – will capture the true economic return.The research outlines five essential pillars that determine whether an organisation successfully scales automation or remains trapped in pilot phases. Despite two-thirds of executives expecting to manage collaborative human-robot teams by 2030, just four in ten have established the structural blueprints necessary to govern them.About 67% of leaders expect automation to upskill human employees—not devalue them. However, 40% say severe talent and skills shortages are currently hindering scaling efforts. Automation’s biggest dividend is workplace safety, according to 31% of respondents, but 55% of them acknowledge that safety concerns have delayed projects. Sixty-eight percent say common international safety standards would speed up implementation.Nearly 77% prefer functional reliability over visual design but 65% believe that modern physical robot designs are constrained by hardware limitations rather than operational needs More than three-quarters of leaders say mission-critical tasks require response times of less than 100 milliseconds, with almost a quarter needing to be executed in less than 10 milliseconds. Currently, 42% have defined funding for edge and on-device AI architectures, and 39% are developing their strategy.
Article Summary: Intel report highlights disconnect between fleet ambition and planning for robots. 60% of senior executives anticipate running active fleets of robots within the next five years. Only 40% currently maintain a documented, formal human-robot workforce framework. Only 42% have defined funding for edge and on- device AI architectures.

Article Title: FTC urged to investigate AI companies over ‘buying and destroying books to train models’
Article Text:
As artificial intelligence companies seek vast quantities of human-written content, concerns are mounting over reports that some rare books are being dismantled and digitised for AI training.

What the letter says

A coalition of over a dozen advocacy and civil society groups has reportedly urged the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to launch a formal inquiry into major artificial intelligence (AI) companies for allegedly purchasing, scanning and physically destroying print books to train their machine learning systems. In a joint petition initially obtained by Axios, organisations including the Consumer Federation of America, Demand Progress Education Fund and the Institute for Local Self-Reliance asked federal regulators to inspect what they describe as a destructive and aggressive data collection method employed by entrenched AI market leaders.The report says that if the FTC acts on the request, the regulatory debate surrounding training data could transition from intellectual property disputes into an antitrust and market competition battle under which, federal regulators would evaluate whether major tech companies are intentionally eliminating physical source material to deny upstart competitors the resources needed to build rival systems.Citing court records, The Washington Post reported in January that AI developer Anthropic expended millions of dollars purchasing books, stripping their spines to digitize the pages, and feeding the text into its Claude model. The publication noted that Google, OpenAI and Microsoft have faced comparable copyright challenges.The letter warns that this tactic threatens to permanently erase rare and out-of-print volumes from the public domain, as technology corporations acquire and scrap the final remaining print editions.The petition argues that purchasing and destroying print media represents an unfair method of competition designed to starve the wider market of essential training inputs.“We urge the FTC to view this practice not in isolation but rather as the latest escalation in a documented pattern of anticompetitive conduct designed to create an insurmountable systemic moat around AI incumbents,” the groups wrote.The coalition explained that unlike conventional data collection, this “hoard-and-destroy” approach functions as an artificial economic barrier, increasing operating costs for smaller entrants and cutting off emerging startups from the underlying content required to compete.
Article Summary: A coalition of over a dozen advocacy and civil society groups has reportedly urged the US Federal Trade Commission to launch a formal inquiry into major artificial intelligence (AI) companies. The petition argues that purchasing and destroying print media represents an unfair method of competition designed to starve the wider market of essential training inputs.

Article Title: How AI memory boom is creating hundreds of millionaires in 1350 kilometres away from Silicon Valley in Idaho
Article Text:
PC: Nasa

Local expansion and economic impact

Located roughly 1,350 kilometres away from Silicon Valley, the Mountain West city of Boise is experiencing a surge in wealth creation, areport has said. Fueled by increasing global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware, local memory chipmaker Micron has seen its market value cross $1 trillion, minting hundreds of new millionaires among long-term employees and area residents. According to a report by CNBC, local financial advisor Dave Petso, who has managed assets in Boise for 45 years through the dot-com crash and the 2008 recession, previously considered the hometown semiconductor manufacturer an unexciting corporate operation and a poor investment.Following a more than ten-fold stock surge since late 2024, Petso spends much of his time helping local clients diversify portfolios that previously held $20,000 in equity and are now worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars.The influx of capital is reshaping Boise, a community of 250,000 traditionally known for outdoor recreation and Boise State University's blue turf football field. Micron has started construction on two local fabrication facilities projected to generate over 17,000 regional jobs, including 3,500 direct roles at Micron, which already employs roughly 7,000 workers locally.The company has also announced the establishment of Micron Research Labs in Boise, backed by a $10 billion investment over the next ten years, with construction starting next year.Meanwhile, Meta is constructing an $800 million data facility in nearby Kuna, Idaho, while key suppliers such as Lam Research and cleanroom contractor Exyte are opening regional offices.Rapid industrial expansion has created growing pains for long-term residents. Locals complain of severe traffic congestion, rising property prices and an influx of newcomers who are reportedly altering local culture.Citing data from leading real estate marketplace Zillow, the report says that average rents in Boise increased 4.3% over the past year while the nationwide rates declined. Resident and tech entrepreneur Jason Crawforth noted that while stock gains have increased his net worth, the rising costs are eroding the low cost of living that once served as the city’s primary competitive advantage.
Article Summary: Micron has seen its market value cross $1 trillion, minting hundreds of new millionaires among long-term employees and area residents. Micron has started construction on two local fabrication facilities projected to generate over 17,000 regional jobs. Locals complain of severe traffic congestion, rising property prices and an influx of newcomers who are altering local culture.

Article Title: Anthropic is about to sell you the company it keeps warning you about
Article Text:
Anthropic accounts for around 60% of the combined revenue estimate of Starbucks and McDonald's

The warnings that built the company become paperwork the moment they are filed

The men warning about concentrated power are about to concentrate some

The forecast and the warning describe the same two years

The contradiction does not get resolved, only priced

Every company that goes public has to write down all the ways it might destroy itself.It is called the risk factors section. It runs for dozens of pages, it is written by lawyers, and almost nobody reads it. Bankers tolerate it. Investors skip past it to the growth charts. It exists so that when something goes badly wrong three years later, the company can point at page 47 and say the warning was always there, in the document you signed off on.Anthropic has been reading its risk factors section out loud for five years.That is the peculiar thing about what is coming. Anthropic expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX's record IPO, according to Bloomberg, and could file publicly as soon as the end of this month. SpaceX raised $75 billion at the outset, rising to $86.2 billion once the overallotment was exercised, the biggest first-time share sale ever recorded.Anthropic is running the numbers on doing that or better, with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase on the deal. The Wall Street Journal puts the debut at September or early October. The last private round, in May, valued the company at $965 billion. It was founded in 2021.None of that is the contradiction. Enormous IPOs happen. Fast growth happens, though rarely at this speed. The contradiction is that Anthropic's whole reason for existing as a separate company from the one its founders walked out of rests on the argument that this technology is dangerous enough to require restraint. And restraint is the one thing a public market does not know how to price.It helps to be precise about what Anthropic sells, because it is not only software. Dario Amodei left OpenAI in 2021 and built a company around a claim: that frontier AI is powerful enough to be hazardous, that the people building it should say so plainly, and that a lab willing to slow itself down is a lab worth trusting with the hard stuff.He has said versions of this on podcasts, in essays, in front of lawmakers, at his own company's Builder Summit in Bengaluru in February. Last week Anthropic published a substantive risk report, per The Information, laying out what its researchers are finding about models that scheme and work against the goals assigned to them. That is not a document most companies publish weeks before the largest IPO in history.And it worked. Not despite the warnings. Because of them. The safety framing is what made Anthropic the vendor cautious enterprises and regulated industries could sign with, and the numbers are the proof.CNBC has confirmed the annualised revenue run rate hit $65 billion at the end of July, a sevenfold jump in a year, up from roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025. Second-quarter revenue crossed $11.5 billion against $787 million a year earlier. OpenAI, over the same three months, booked $6.7 billion.Then the prospectus lands, and every one of those warnings changes function.They stop being conviction and become legal artefacts, restated in the flat defensive register of securities law. Risks related to our models. Risks related to our regulatory environment. Once a warning sits in that section it is no longer a signal of seriousness, it is a shield against being sued for the thing you warned about.The audience changes with it. For five years Amodei was talking to governments, researchers and the public. From the day of the filing he is talking to shareholders, a constituency with exactly one question, asked quarterly.The financials make that question sharp. Anthropic posted a net loss of almost $42 billion in 2025, roughly five times the year before, on revenue of about $10 billion, according to documents seen by Bloomberg. Reuters has the second quarter delivering a first operating profit of $559 million, which is a real turn.But the spending behind those losses has not slowed. One compute agreement with SpaceX alone could be worth tens of billions of dollars over three years. A company burning at that scale has very little room to make an expensive decision on principle, and even less once the burn is public.Anthropic knows all of this. You can tell, because of what it is building to defend itself.The company has been preparing a class of stock with extra voting power for Amodei and his six co-founders, The Information first revealed, which would be the first time Anthropic's leaders held voting rights beyond their ownership. The mechanism is ordinary in Silicon Valley. Meta, Snap and SpaceX all did it.What makes it unusual here is the arithmetic. Amodei owns about 2 percent of the company he founded, a person close to it told the same publication, his stake diluted by hundreds of billions in outside capital. That may be the smallest founder holding of any chief executive taking a company public in decades.Sitting alongside it is the Long-Term Benefit Trust, created in 2023, holding Class T shares with no economic value and one real power: electing the majority of Anthropic's seven-person board. Ben Bernanke is a trustee. The trust is currently down to three members from its usual five, after Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar left this month to become Anthropic's chief global affairs officer.Read that structure plainly and it is an admission. Anthropic is inviting the public markets in and bolting the doors from the inside on the way. Supervoting shares insulate the founders from shareholder pressure. The trust keeps the board.The company also stays a public benefit corporation, legally permitted to weigh society against returns, which will make it by an enormous margin the largest such entity on any US exchange. The next biggest is Veeva Systems, at $40 billion.Amodei's defence writes itself, and it is not a bad one: the point of the shares is to protect the mission from precisely the short-term pressure the listing invites. But a man who has spent years warning that AI risks concentrating power in too few hands is about to be handed more of it.You also cannot argue that outside shareholders will push a company toward decisions it should not make and simultaneously argue that selling them the company is fine. Both cannot be true. The governance structure is Anthropic conceding the first one.The valuation math tells you what investors are actually buying, and it is not caution. Anthropic is projecting 2028 revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters has learnt, with bankers valuing the company off that number two years out. The comparison set includes Palantir, which trades at 53 times this year's expected revenue, and Cloudflare and SpaceX, both around 41 times.Apply anything like those multiples and a $2 trillion debut stops being a fantasy. That is roughly where one investor landed when the news agency asked him, his question being not whether Anthropic could get there but whether it would stay.Hold that forecast against the safety argument. To go from $65 billion annualised to $200 billion booked inside two and a half years, Claude has to be inside almost everything, including healthcare and biology, which is where the company has told investors it plans to push next.That is not a scenario with a pause in it. That is maximum deployment at maximum speed, in exactly the window Amodei has described as the one where models get capable enough to be dangerous.He has already shown what a pause costs. In June, Anthropic temporarily disabled access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 to comply with a US export control directive citing national security authorities, and got them back roughly two weeks later after tense negotiation and some concessions.Earlier this year the Pentagon blacklisted the company after talks over military use collapsed on the limits Anthropic wanted, and the two sides are still in court. Investors have been pressing executives on exactly this in pre-IPO meetings, the Journal found, alongside cheap Chinese models and the backlash to data centre construction.Anthropic absorbed all of it as a private company, because the only people owed an explanation were investors already committed and reachable in a room. Do the same fortnight as a listed company and it is a material event, a stock move, a set of analyst notes, and a class of shareholders asking why management picked a fight it could have avoided.The willingness to lose money over a limit is what made the safety position credible. After the listing, that willingness has a price, it is visible to everyone, and somebody will eventually argue in court that paying it was a breach of duty.Both things stay true, and one of them starts trading. The safety mission is not being abandoned, and the people running Anthropic are not cynics who stopped believing their own case. But an IPO does one thing above all others. It converts a private conviction into a number that trades, and hands the number to strangers.Anthropic has spent five years telling the world this technology is too important to be governed by people chasing quarterly returns. In September or October it will sell that world a large stake in itself and invite exactly those people to the table.The supervoting shares, the trust, the benefit corporation charter are all attempts to take the capital without the consequence. They will hold, or they will not. Nobody knows yet, because the first real test has not arrived.But it will. There will come a quarter when the safe decision and the profitable one point in opposite directions, and unlike every previous instance, the whole market will be watching which way Anthropic goes. Every buyer will have been warned before that quarter arrives, by the people who stand to make the most from being wrong.Anthropic said it out loud for five years. From the filing onwards, it says it on page 47.
Article Summary: Anthropic has been reading its risk factors section out loud for five years. The company has been preparing a class of stock with extra voting power. It could file publicly as soon as the end of this month. Anthropic expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX's record IPO.
